title: Data Governance & Access Control
summary: Who can see which rows and columns, whether "de-identified" data actually is, and what right-to-deletion means in a warehouse built to never delete — these are engineering decisions, not just legal ones.

slides.markdown:
[Catalogs](data-catalogs-metadata) make data findable. Governance decides who's actually allowed to see what, once they've found it — and it's a genuine engineering discipline, not a legal afterthought bolted on at the end.

The core pieces: classifying which columns are sensitive, enforcing row- and column-level visibility per role, choosing the right technique for de-identifying data, and designing pipelines that can honor obligations like right-to-deletion even when the storage model wasn't built with deletion in mind.

slides.sectionTitle: Why this is a data-engineering concern
slides.markdown:
It's tempting to treat "who can see this data" as purely a legal or compliance question, answered once in a policy document. In practice, every enforcement mechanism — row filters, column masks, access grants — lives in the pipelines and warehouse configuration that data engineers build and maintain, which makes governance an engineering responsibility whether or not it's labeled that way.

A policy that says "only finance can see salary data" does nothing on its own; someone has to implement the specific row/column security rule that actually enforces it, keep it correct as the schema evolves, and make sure a well-meaning new pipeline doesn't accidentally expose the same data through a side door — a new report, a data export, a copy into a less-restricted table.

slides.subTitle: Identifying sensitive columns systematically
slides.markdown:
**PII (personally identifiable information) classification** means tagging every column that could identify a real person — name, email, SSN, precise location, and less obvious ones like a device ID or an IP address that can often be linked back to a person.

Doing this systematically, not by memory, matters because "I'll remember which columns are sensitive" doesn't survive organizational turnover or a warehouse with thousands of columns. Classification is usually a mix of automated pattern detection (a column matching an email or SSN format gets auto-flagged) and manual review for less obvious cases, then recorded as catalog metadata so every downstream consumer — and every access-control rule — can reference the same classification rather than each team re-deciding independently.

**Row-level security** restricts which *rows* of a table a given user or role can see — a regional sales manager queries the same `fct_sales` table as everyone else, but the policy transparently filters results to only their region's rows. **Column-level security** restricts which *columns* are visible — an analyst can query the customer table and see name and region, but a `salary` or `ssn` column returns null or is masked, for the exact same query, based on their role.

The defining feature of both is that they're enforced by the warehouse itself at query time, not by each report author remembering to add the right `WHERE` clause or leave out the right column — which means the policy holds even against a query nobody anticipated writing.

slides.sectionTitle: A masking policy at query time
slides.markdown:
The same underlying table, queried by two different roles, returns different results for the sensitive column — the masking decision happens inside the warehouse's query execution, based on who's asking, not by maintaining two separate copies of the table.

![Same query and table producing masked or unmasked salary values depending on role](assets/masked-column-access.svg)

slides.markdown:
**Data minimization** is the principle of collecting and retaining only what's actually needed, not "everything, in case it's useful someday." **Retention policies** operationalize this by defining, per dataset, how long data is kept before it's automatically deleted or anonymized — raw clickstream events might be retained for 90 days, while aggregated, non-identifying metrics derived from them are kept indefinitely.

The engineering discipline this requires: retention can't be a policy document nobody enforces — it needs an actual scheduled job that deletes or anonymizes data past its retention window, and a way to verify that job is actually running and covering every dataset it's supposed to, not just the ones someone remembered to configure.

| | Anonymization | Pseudonymization | Tokenization |
|---|---|---|---|
| What happens | Identifying information is irreversibly removed or generalized | A direct identifier is replaced with a consistent artificial identifier, with a way back via a separate mapping | A sensitive value is replaced with a non-sensitive token, with the real value stored separately in a secure vault |
| Reversible? | No, by design | Yes, if you have access to the mapping | Yes, if you have access to the vault |
| Re-identification risk | Should be genuinely low if done correctly | Real — anyone with the mapping can re-identify | Real — anyone with vault access can retrieve the original |
| Typical use | Public research datasets, aggregated reporting | Analytics where you need to track "the same user" across events without exposing who they are | Payment card numbers, other regulated fields needing a secure, retrievable original |

The critical distinction for governance purposes: only anonymization is meant to make re-identification impossible. Pseudonymization and tokenization are both reversible by design for whoever holds the mapping or vault — treating either of them as equivalent to "anonymous" for compliance purposes is a real, common mistake.

A dataset has names and emails removed and gets labeled "de-identified." It still has ZIP code, birth date, and gender — and a well-known finding in privacy research showed that combination alone uniquely identifies a large majority of the U.S. population when cross-referenced against publicly available records like voter rolls.

The mistake is treating de-identification as "remove the obviously identifying columns" rather than actually reasoning about **re-identification risk** — what could this data be joined against, and does the *combination* of remaining fields, even without any single obviously-identifying column, narrow down to a specific person? A dataset can pass a naive "no name, no email" checklist and still be trivially re-identifiable, which is exactly why real anonymization work requires actually modeling the re-identification risk, not just deleting a column list.

Regulations like GDPR and CCPA grant individuals a right to have their personal data deleted on request. Many analytics warehouses are architecturally built around append-only, immutable data — [Type 2 SCDs](slowly-changing-dimensions) deliberately keep every historical version, and some storage formats favor write-once patterns for performance and auditability.

Those two things are in real tension: a warehouse optimized to never overwrite history has to somehow support surgically removing one specific person's data from every table and every historical version they ever appeared in, without breaking the aggregates and joins built on top. This isn't a solved problem with one standard answer — approaches range from tombstone records that null out PII fields while preserving row structure, to periodic reprocessing jobs that rebuild affected tables with the deleted person's data excluded, and the right approach depends heavily on the specific storage format and how aggressively history is actually relied upon downstream.

A junior answer to "how do you handle sensitive data" is "we have a policy that says only certain people can see it." A senior answer names the actual enforcement mechanism — row/column security at query time, systematic PII classification feeding that enforcement, and a real technique (not just "we removed the name column") for any de-identification claim — and can speak to the specific tension between compliance obligations like right-to-deletion and an architecture built around immutable history.

The throughline across this entire group: governance, quality, contracts, lineage, and access control are all the same underlying idea applied to different failure modes — make an implicit assumption explicit, and enforce it mechanically rather than trusting it to hold by convention.

This topic covered controlling access to data that's already known to exist and be sensitive. The final topic in this group covers the complementary problem: noticing when a pipeline itself is broken — stale, missing rows, schema drift — continuously, rather than only discovering it when a quality check happens to fire or a stakeholder complains.
